questions.questionText: Amid global economic uncertainties, India’s Balance of Payments (BoP) has shown remarkable  resilience. Elaborate on the factors contributing to this stability.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of global economic uncertainties and India’s external sector resilience.
• In the body, discuss the factors contributing to India’s Balance of Payments (BoP) stability.
• Conclude by providing suggestions to maintain this stability. | | --- | As per **Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index**, the world faces rising political and economic uncertainty due to **geopolitical conflicts (**Russia-Ukraine war, West Asia conflict), **geoeconomic fragmentation (**trade wars), and **extreme climate events** (heatwaves). The **2024 "Great Election Year"** (affecting over half the world's population) added to **policy unpredictability**. Amidst these global economic uncertainties, India’s Balance of Payments (BoP) has shown remarkable **resilience.** This is on account of the following **factors**: 1. a) Stable current account deficit** despite increase in merchandise trade deficit (due to rise in net services receipt);** b) substantial **private transfers (**with remittances reaching $31.9 billion in Q2 FY25), reflecting the **economic resilience** of the Indian diaspora. 2. a) **FDI inflows have remained resilient** (YoY growth ~18% till Nov 2024) driven by India’s **robust** **economic fundamentals**, ongoing **structural reforms (**GST rationalization), and growing consumer base; b) **reversal** of the trend of **FPI outflows** and **upward trend in** External Commercial Borrowing **(ECBs)** due to long-term attractiveness of Indian equity markets (highlighted by ES 2024-25). 3. a) **Low external debt-to-GDP ratio** (19.4% in Sept 2024) and a **decline** in the share of **short-term debt** therein (19.4% to 18.8% between June to Sept 2024); b) high **forex reserves** (~$654billion, March 2025), providing **buffer** against external shocks. 4. a) **Inclusion of Indian Bonds** in **Global Indices** (JP Morgan Index) boosted foreign investment and capital inflows; c) growth in **NRI deposits** (owing to favourable exchange rate environment), further strengthening reserves. 5. a) Long-term measures** aimed at promoting **export competitiveness** (RoDTEP scheme, Dak Niryat Kendras) and enhanced **market access** (trade agreements with UAE, Australia);** b) efforts aimed at **reducing import dependence** (SPRs, renewable energy push, NMEO-Oilseeds). Amid **uncertainties over global trade policies** (e.g., potential tariff wars under the new U.S. administration), India must safeguard BoP stability. This can be achieved by adopting a **strategic trade roadmap** aimed at enhancing export competitiveness, reducing import dependence, and **deepening global supply chain** **integration.** ***(317 words)*** **RoDTEP:** Remission of Taxes and Duties on Exported Products**; SPR:** Strategic Petroleum Reserves**; NMEO-** **Oilseeds:** National Mission on Edible Oils- Oilseeds

questions.questionText: The economic reforms of 1991 significantly reshaped India’s economic landscape. Elaborate on the  need for these reforms and their key objectives.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about the economic reforms of.
• In the body, first elaborate on the need for these reforms, and then discuss their key objectives. Conclude by highlighting the need for Reforms. | | --- | The economic reforms of 1991 entailed an **overhaul** of Indian economy in alignment with **market principles.** They marked a departure from the **post-independence economic model** (socialistic pattern, import substitution) towards the IMF-sponsored **Structural Adjustment Programme.** **Need** for these reforms arose due to the following challenges: 1. Changing **global economic conditions** post the **decline of communism** in Eastern Europe (drop in aid available to developing countries). This forced a **rethink** on India’s own **economic strategy** (inspired by the Soviet model) and the need to align with the **emerging global economic consensus**. 2. **Balance of Payment crisis (1990-91)** caused due to trade imbalances, declining remittances post- Gulf war etc. This triggered a sharp **decline in the forex reserves** (import cover declined to 2-3 weeks). 3. a) Progressive deterioration in **macro-economic fundamentals** (fiscal deficit, persistent inflation) led to a **downgrade in credit ratings** (made external borrowing costlier); b) overhanging effects of post- independence economic policies **(industrial licensing, production controls, import substitution**) undermined India’s **economic competitiveness** (low technological base of manufacturing, subscale businesses). 4. a) Pervasive inefficiencies in the **public sector** due to lack of effective **competition** from the private sector; b) myriad **bureaucratic frameworks** (permissions, inspection) giving rise to problems like **rent-** **seeking, red-tapism**. The key **objectives** of the economic reforms of 1991: 1. a) Resolution of BoP** situation through **foreign exchange reforms (**devaluation of rupee, rupee convertibility**); b) liberalization of trade policy** to enhance **competitiveness** of domestic manufacturing (new technologies) and develop India’s **consumer market.**** 2. a) Macro-economic stabilization** by restoring **fiscal discipline** (containing government expenditure and raising revenue);** b) **rapid industrial development** through de-regulation (abolition of licensing requirements, removal of price controls). 3. a) Financial sector reforms** (private banks, FDI in banking) to expand the **resource base** of banks and **ease credit access**;** b) development of a broad-based **capital market** in the country (permitting foreign institutional investors); c) **strengthening capital market regulations** (statutory status to the SEBI). 4. a) Taxation reforms (**lower rates, procedural simplification) to encourage **savings** and promote **voluntary disclosure of income;**** b) indirect tax reforms to create a **common national market** for goods and services. 5. Reducing the size of the ‘**bloated public sector’ (**privatization) and enhancing its **efficiency** (managerial autonomy). The economic reforms of 1991 laid the foundation for India's transformation, but the journey towards a **'Viksit** **Bharat by 2047'** requires another package of reforms. **Reforms 2.0** (technology upgradation, digitization, land reforms, etc.) need to aim at achieving structural overhaul of India’s economy and be guided by the principles of **inclusivity, sustainability** and **dynamism.** ***(407 words)***

questions.questionText: Elaborate on the various policy instruments available to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for regulating  money supply in the economy. Also, explain why the RBI is known as the ‘lender of last resort’.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer with a brief background about the RBI.
• In the body, elaborate on the various policy instruments available to RBI for regulating money supply in the economy.
• Next, explain why it is termed as the ‘lender of last resort’.
• Conclude by highlighting the significance of RBI in ensuring financial stability and safeguarding depositors' interests. | | --- | The Reserve Bank of India **(RBI)** is the **Central banking authority** in India, established under the **RBI Act, 1934.** Its **key objective**, among others, is to maintain **price stability** while **supporting economic growth**. Different **policy instruments** are available to the RBI for regulating money supply in the economy, as discussed: 1. **Quantitative measures** (alter the money supply in the economy directly) a) Altering **reserve ratios** like **CRR** (4% in Feb 2025), SLR (18% in Feb 2025) which impacts **cash** **in circulation** and **credit availability**. For instance, a reduction of CRR/ SLR is likely to boost money supply in the economy. b) i) **Liquidity Adjustment Facility** (LAF) instruments like **Repo (**6.25% in Feb 2025**), Reverse** **repo rates (**3.35% in Feb 2025) and **Standing Deposit Facility** (6% in Feb 2025). They primarily help the RBI maintain **short-term liquidity** by injecting or absorbing funds in the banking system. ii) **long-term** liquidity needs are met through **Long-Term Repo Operations (**LTROs**)** which provide 1-3-year loans to banks. c) Other mechanism like i) **Bank rate** (6.5% in Feb 2025) when **no collateral** is involved (lending occurs through discounting bills of exchange); ii) **Marginal Standing Facility** (6.5% in Feb 2025) when banks are short of securities above SLR limit; iii) **Open Market Operations** (to inject durable liquidity in the banking system (e.g. Operation Twist 2019) and **Market** **Stabilization Schemes.** 2. **Qualitative Measure**s (alter the money supply **indirectly**) a) i) **Credit rationing** by fixing limits to certain sectors, e.g. CRAR framework, Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms; ii) varying **margin requirements** for different sectors. b) i) Regulation of **consumer credit** through adjusting minimum down payment and period of repayment; ii) **moral suasion** to make banks adhere to its policies and directives. c) **Direct action** like placing under Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework (Allahabad Bank) or imposing **moratorium on lending (**Yes Bank). RBI is termed as the '**lender of last resort**' because it can extend **credit to a bank** (that is solvent but faces temporary liquidity challenges) when **no one else is willing** to lend to it. For e.g., RBI extended Rs **60000-crore** **credit line** to **Yes Bank** during the 2020 crisis. Thus, the RBI employs a **mix of quantitative and qualitative instruments** to regulate the money supply and ensure financial stability. As the **lender of last resort**, its role is to provide emergency **liquidity to solvent bank**s facing crises, safeguarding depositors’ interests and the banking system. ***(397 words)***
